signalslink:block-handbooktext-blocksens:
The block sensor detects the presence of a block at a selected adjacent position and, based on its type or input signal, provides information about its state or slot occupancy at the output.
The currently supported blocks are:
Anvil - if there is a sufficiently hot ingot on the anvil for forging, the Output signal is 1. Otherwise, it sends signal 0.
Doors, gates, trapdoors - For doors and gates, you need to monitor the block at ground level on the hinge side. If the block is open, the Output signal is 1; if it is closed, the Output signal is 0.
A chest or any container in general, or any blocks that have inventory slots (e.g. a campfire, barrel, trough, etc.). The Output signal is determined by the input signal.
The input signal determines which slot is to be scanned.
Signals 1-14 specify slots 0-13. The output is information about the occupancy of the slot relative to the maximum stack capacity of the item in that slot, converted to a signal from 0-15.
Signal 15 specifies that the sensor should detect the total occupancy of all slots, e.g. the entire chest.
Any other block not listed above - If there is nothing in the monitored area (there is air), the Output signal is 0. If there is water, the output is 2-fresh water or 3-salt water. If there is any other block, the Output signal is 1.

Paper Conditions
Paper Conditions are relevant to the block sensor when monitoring containers or blocks with inventories in general. If you have set Paper Conditions, the behavior of the block sensor changes as follows: If you are monitoring a specific slot (input signal 1-14), the conditions are applied to the item in that slot and, if it matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If output is not specified, signal 15 is returned.
If you are monitoring the total inventory occupancy (input signal 15), the conditions are applied to all items in all monitored slots. As soon as an item matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If the output instruction is not specified in the conditions, the number of the first slot where a match was found is returned.
Tip: You can use this to find out the slot number. Place an item in the slot whose number you want to know. Leave the other slots empty, then monitor this block with a block sensor to which you apply the paper condition "*" and send signal 15 to its input. The output will then be the signal with the number of the slot containing the item.
If no item in the slots matches the Paper Conditions, signal 0 is returned.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-entitysen:
The Entity Sensor detects the presence of entities (players, livestock, wild animals, or monsters) in the marked area and can provide information on its outputs about their count, type, or status. The sensor requires charging with one or more Temporal Gears to operate. The consumption rate then depends on the size of the monitored area.
Inputs x, y, z determine the size of the monitored area in blocks.
On the Error output there is signal 1 if the sensor is discharged, otherwise 0.
Inputs Output 1 setting and Output 2 setting determine what information will be provided on outputs 1 and 2. You can thus obtain different information on each output, based on these input settings.
The options are:
1 - The output returns Count. The number of detected entities.
2 - The output returns Category. Bit flags of entity category 0–3: player, creature, animal, wild animal.
3 - The output returns Life state. All detected entities are: 1–dead, 2–alive, or 15–mixed.
4 - The output returns Sex. All detected entities are: 1–male, 2–female, or 15–mixed.
5 - The output returns Age. All detected entities are: 1–young, 2–adult, or 15–mixed.
6 - The output returns Species. All detected entities are: 1–player, 2–animal, 3–wild animal, 4–creature, or 15–mixed.
7 - The output returns Reproductive state. All detected entities are: 1–ready to mate, 2–pregnant, 3–lactating, or 15–mixed.
8 - The output returns Reproductive state flags. Bit flags 0–2: ready to mate, pregnant, lactating.
9 - The output returns Minimum generation. The minimum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
10 - The output returns Maximum generation. The maximum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
11 - The output returns Minimum weight. The minimum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
12 - The output returns Maximum weight. The maximum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedch:
The Managed Chute enables automated item transport between different blocks. It transports items in only one direction, marked on the chute by a white arrow.
Unlike a chute, the Managed Chute has no inventory of its own and transports items from the block on the source side directly into the block on the target side. This means items are not stored in the chute, but merely transferred through it.
The Managed Chute has four Signals connectors: Input, Source, Target, and Output.
• Input controls transport. If the Input signal is 0, the chute is inactive and transports no items. A non-zero value at the input triggers transport of items from source to target. The following input values are supported:
1 - Transport one item
2 - Transport 2 items
3 - Transport 4 items
4 - Transport 8 items
5 - Transport 16 items
6 - Transport 32 items
7 - Transport 64 items
15 - Transport continuously.
Input values 1-7 allow items to be transported in batches. If the source block does not contain enough items to transport the requested amount, the chute transports as much as it can and moves the remainder only when another signal appears at the input. To transport another amount, different signal values from 1 to 7 can be sent to the input successively to compose the desired batch size.
Input value 15 causes the chute to continuously transport items from source to target, regardless of how many items need to be transported. The chute continues transporting items as soon as they appear in the source, until the input signal changes to another value.
Transport occurs when something is available for transport on the source side and there is room to store items on the target side. If either condition is not met, the chute attempts to transport items, but if this is not possible, it remains inactive until the situation changes (for example, items appear in the source or space is freed at the target).
• Source is relevant when the input block is a block with an inventory. In that case, the signal at Source determines which slot items are taken from. Signals 1-14 select slots 0-13. Signal 15 means items are taken from the last slot.
Signal 0 means items are taken from any slot. In this case, the chute searches all slots and takes items from the first non-empty slot. If the source block has no inventory, this input is ignored.
• Target is relevant when the output block is a block with an inventory or air. For an inventory, the signal at Target determines which slot items are placed into. Signals 1-15 select slots 0-14.
If the target block is air and there is ground beneath it, the following Target values are relevant: 1 - the chute attempts to place a block from the source onto the ground, 2 - the chute attempts to place an item on the ground if it can be placed. Signal 2 can also place a bucket including its contents; the bucket is not emptied.
The target ground directive on paper forces this attempt regardless of the Target signal. It first attempts to place a block or bucket, then possibly creates an item pile.
• Output reports what the chute sees at its ends. It is zero by default; its value is supplied by blocks with the output directive in Paper Conditions. Besides transport, the chute therefore also acts as a sensor and can control other machines.
Piles on the ground
The chute stores stackable items — such as firewood, ingots, boards, and others that can be piled on the ground — in piles. It creates a pile itself even on an empty spot and continues adding to it. A pile's capacity is determined by the item, not its stack size: one pile of ingots holds 64 pieces, even though ingots stack in chests in groups of 16.
When a pile is full, the target ground N directive allows it to continue one block higher, up to N blocks above the target position. The column stops at a solid block or when the new pile lacks support beneath it. Without a number, only the target block is filled.
Collecting from the ground works in reverse: the chute takes from the top of the column and removes emptied piles, so the column is dismantled from top to bottom.
Both operations can work in batches; see amount N below.

It can also collect layered blocks, such as fired charcoal. This is not an item pile, so the chute dismantles it layer by layer from the top. Conditions see such a column as an inventory, so its contents can be queried just like a chest.

If the source block is air, the chute collects floating items from a 3x3-block area whose middle block is the block in front of the chute opening. It can also pick up a bucket standing directly in front of the opening and insert it into the target inventory including its contents.

Building a firepit
The target firepit directive at the target position does not build a firepit from a finished block, but gradually as a player would: first dry grass, then sticks, and finally firewood. Each time, the chute takes only the material actually required by the next construction phase, so it does not stuff firewood into an unfinished firepit before there is anything to light it with.
A finished firepit is an ordinary target with an inventory, so fuel is added by normal transfer. It can then be lit by the Igniter.

Besides the above, the Managed Chute can also insert items of the type Ingot, Iron Bloom, and Blister Steel into an anvil if the anvil is placed on the chute's target side. When it inserts ingots onto an anvil, the plate forging recipe is selected automatically. For Iron Bloom and Blister Steel, slag forging is selected so that they become ingots. This is very useful for automating forging with an automatic hammer. Before inserting them onto the anvil, however, you must ensure that the inserted items are heated to the temperature required for forging. Conditions see the anvil as an inventory with one slot containing its workpiece. Therefore the in target scope works on it, including inventoryEmpty and inventoryFilled. The amount N directive inserts N pieces and is atomic: either all are inserted, or none are inserted and nothing is removed from the source.

Transport filtering
The Managed Chute allows conditions to be set for filtering items to be transported. Conditions are configured using Paper Conditions, whose use is explained on this page
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedwa:
A Managed Chute embedded in a wall enables automated transport of items between various blocks. It allows transporting items through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for moving items from a cellar or into a cellar without disturbing the cool cellar environment, important for long-term food storage.
It works on the same principle as the Managed Chute. You can therefore find the usage description on the page describing the Managed Chute.
signalslink:usageinfo-signalslink-text:
SignalsLink
Extends the Signals mod with additional components.

To monitor a nearby block, you can use a Block Sensor.
If you need to monitor your herd of livestock, the Entity Sensor is ideal.
If you want to automate some work, the Managed Chute serves you well. It can move items between blocks similarly to a chute, but you control it with signals and gain much greater control over what is transported. Its Managed Chute built into a wall variant lets you transport items through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for transporting items from or into a cellar without disrupting the cool cellar environment important for long-term food preservation.

The Managed Damper, connected by a sleeve, moves items over longer distances and through ceilings or floors. Extend the line with sleeve couplings. To pass through a wall, use a wall sleeve coupling. The damper can also place cargo on the ground and pick it up again, so it is useful anywhere a chute cannot reach.

The Managed Valve is used to transport liquids. Connect it with a hose to another valve or to a water intake in water; build a longer line using hose couplings.

The Freight Dock handles loading and unloading. It is a crate that finds what stands beside it — a boat, pack animal, and, with the appropriate add-on, a train — and transfers goods wherever its paper tells it to. It can also stack goods on a storage yard: continuous paving that it treats as one store and that you name with a storage yard sign.

The Igniter lights fires remotely. It fires a burst of sparks on a signal and ignites whatever it points at, so it can light a firepit without you standing there.

To keep a remote factory running even when nobody is nearby, build a Chunk Anchor next to it. It keeps a selected part of the world loaded, pays temporal gears based on how much it keeps alive, and can sleep between shifts to save gears.

You control the behaviour of all this equipment with Paper Conditions, which are shared by all of them.
signalslink:usageinfo-paperconditions-te:
Conditions on paper are a shared rules system for Managed Chutes, Managed Dampers, Managed Valves, Freight Docks, and sensors. Write rules on parchment and insert it into a supported device.
All these devices work the same way: they have the same syntax, the same evaluation process, and the same meaning of Output. They differ only in what their source and destination are and what they can do.

Basic principle
One paragraph on parchment forms one block. Separate blocks with one or more blank lines. Lines beginning with # or // are comments and are ignored.
All conditions in one block must be true at the same time (AND). Blocks are processed from top to bottom.
Sections with a header. A Freight Dock has two ends and therefore divides its paper into sections. Each section starts with a header, such as load yard or from yard to boat, which says where goods go from and to. The header is on its own line, separated from the blocks below by a blank line, and applies until the next header. How headers are written and what they can name is described under Freight Dock. Other devices have their source and destination determined by where they stand and do not use headers.
Mind the AND. Two conditions on the same code do not override each other; both must apply. This is useful: game:planks 5+ and game:planks 20- in one block mean between five and twenty. But it also means that one impossible line kills the entire block. A classic case is game:planks * with a space: it looks like planks in any quantity, but it is a pattern for a code containing a space, and no such code exists. The paper warns you about this; see Errors on paper below.

How paper is evaluated
One top-to-bottom pass does two things at once: determines the Output value and performs an action, meaning a transfer or do seal.
This also divides blocks into types. A block with the output directive is an output block and transfers nothing; every other block is an action block. One pass can therefore set Output and transfer something at the same time.
Three rules apply:
• The first valid output block wins; later ones are skipped.
• If no output block applies, Output is 0. Output reflects the current state. A paper with no output blocks therefore keeps Output permanently at zero.
• One action per pass is performed: the first action block whose action actually does work. A block that would transfer nothing (empty source, full destination, invalid ifEmpty) falls through to the next block. This is what makes chains of blocks with target N ifEmpty work, filling one slot after another.
Order matters. Actions change the state of the destination, so the same output block above an action and below it answers differently in the same tick. It is up to you where you write it.
Likewise, block order takes precedence over slot order: a block higher on the paper searches all slots it may use before allowing a block below it to act. The paper decides priority, not the layout of the chest.
A pass runs on every work tick of the device, even when it currently has no input signal, has nothing to transfer, or is waiting for its turn. This means every device with an output block also acts as a sensor.

Devices and actions
• A Managed Chute transfers items between the blocks at its two ends. It supports source, target, target ground, target firepit, amount, keep, ifEmpty, do seal, and output.
• A Managed Damper transfers items through its sleeve and supports the same directives as a chute. However, it has no Source and Target pins, so slot selection and ground mode are set only through directives.
• A Managed Valve transfers liquids from the distant end of its hose to its host. It supports source, target, amount, keep (in litres), ifEmpty, do seal, and output. It does not transfer lava and cools hot water at the destination.
• A Freight Dock transfers goods between its crate and what stands beside it: a storage yard, boat, or elk. It divides paper into sections with headers. Without amount, it transfers everything matching the rule in one operation. It supports amount, keep, height, and output.
• Sensors transfer nothing; their default action is signal output. Every one of their blocks is therefore an output block even if you omit output; they additionally understand output . for the number of the matching slot.

Code and attribute conditions
Exact code: game:resin. An asterisk * replaces any number of characters, and a question mark ? one character: game:log-placed-*, game:ingot-?. A regular expression starts with @, for example @^game:log-placed-(oak|maple)-.*$. The ! prefix negates the entire line, for example !game:resin or !game:firewood 96+.
A valid attribute name checks its truth value. Comparisons use >, >=, <, <=, =, ==: temperature>1100, stackSize>=16, durabilityRatio>=0.75. Also available are temperature, durability, durabilityMax, freshHoursLeft, and isSpoiling.
The isBurning condition asks about a block, not its contents: it applies when that end is burning, such as a lit firepit or a smouldering log pile. It works in both scopes.
A bucket and other liquid containers provide isLiquidContainer, liquidContainerEmpty, liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode, and liquidLitres. For example, a full ten-litre bucket of water matches liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode=game:waterportion, and liquidLitres=10.
For liquids, patterns work on both the world block and the liquid's internal component, for example game:water-*, game:water-still-7, *weaktannin*, or game:waterportion.

Inventory and quantity
inventoryAny condition checks any slot of the selected inventory, for example inventoryAny game:resin. It also checks liquids in liquid slots.
inventoryEmpty applies when the selected inventory is completely empty. inventoryFilled is the opposite, meaning it contains something; it does not mean it is filled to capacity. Both are especially useful with in target, where they check the state of the destination rather than the transferred item.
A pattern quantity condition checks the total quantity in an inventory: game:resin 10 means exactly 10, game:resin 10+ at least 10, and game:resin 10- at most 10. For liquids, quantity is in litres and may have up to two decimal places, for example game:water-* 50 or *weaktannin* 20+.
You can append slot N after a quantity and ask about only one slot rather than the whole inventory: game:firewood 96+ slot 2. Slots are counted from one, just like target N. A slot outside the inventory's range is read as empty.
The difference matters: two slots with fifty logs each total one hundred, so game:firewood 96+ applies, but game:firewood 96+ slot 1 does not.
A condition with a slot is a watcher, not a selector. It asks about an inventory rather than the carried item, so by itself it does not qualify a block for transfer. This lets one block transfer one thing while conditioning it on another.

Scope and transfer
in source switches conditions to the source inventory and is the default. in target switches them to the destination inventory. You can alternate them within one block; a scope applies to the lines following it.
A block that is meant to transfer something must say what, meaning it must have at least one code condition in the source scope. If you do not care what it carries, write *. A block made only of in target conditions would have nothing by which to select items, and the paper reports this. This does not apply to a valve, whose source is the distant end of its hose.
source N selects a source slot and takes priority over the Source pin. target N selects a destination slot, numbered from one. target N ifEmpty requires an empty destination slot; after it is filled, the block falls through to the next one. target ground on a device aimed into air ignores the Target pin and tries to place the item on solid ground; target ground N additionally lets the pile grow up to N blocks above the target position. target firepit builds a firepit at the target position, progressively according to what the next construction stage needs.
amount N sets the size of one batch. For items, a batch is atomic: either all of it is transferred, or nothing is transferred and the block falls through to the next one. A batch can be collected from multiple slots with the same contents. A valve transfers up to the specified amount of liquid according to source, destination, and remaining buffer.
A sign may follow the number. amount N- is a cap: at most N is transferred, and if there are fewer goods, whatever is available is transferred; it never waits. amount N+ is a threshold: it waits until N are available, then takes everything available, up to one stack of that item, or 10 litres for liquids. For example, amount 1+ transfers full stacks whenever there is anything to transfer: stones in stacks of 64, ingots in stacks of 16.
For piles on the ground, batches work in both directions. When placing, they can overflow into a higher pile in the column; when collecting, they are taken across several layers from the top, then distributed over as many destination inventory slots as needed.
keep N says something different from amount: it is a level at the destination, not a batch size. The block delivers only what is missing up to N, and once N is there, it does nothing and falls through to the next block. If something is removed from the destination, it replenishes it. Therefore keep never waits for a full batch and never overshoots — unlike atomic amount N.
Everything the block carries is counted, so game:ingot-* with keep 17 means seventeen ingots total, regardless of their type. It uses the same counting as the condition in target game:ingot-* 17-, so those two lines never contradict each other. For valves, it is counted in litres.
Both can be written together: keep 17 and amount 5 mean "in batches of five until there are seventeen".

Output and sealing
output X sets Output to a value from 0 to 15. Output blocks always ask about the destination, meaning the end where the device itself sits; you do not need to write the in target prefix in them, and in source makes no sense in them.
Resetting is automatic: when no output block applies during a given pass, Output is 0. A resetting output 0 above filling blocks is therefore unnecessary.
do seal seals the destination barrel if it can be sealed. It usually belongs after filling blocks. A sealed barrel cannot be sealed again.

Errors on paper
Paper with an error is still accepted, so one mistyped line does not stop the entire machine. Faulty lines behave as invalid, and errors are reported twice: immediately when attaching the parchment to the block and then permanently in the block's information window, in red above the conditions text.
The message always states the line number and reason. It reports an unknown scope, invalid output, source, target, amount, or slot, an unknown action, an incomprehensible condition, and in source in an output block.
Two messages are worth noting because they reveal paper that looks correct yet silently does nothing: a code pattern with a space and a block that does not say what it should transfer.

Examples
game:log-placed-*
target 3
Transfers wooden logs into slot 3.

game:water-*
target 2 ifEmpty
amount 50

in target
game:water-* 50+
do seal
First fills empty slot 2 with water. Once the slot is no longer empty, the first block falls through and the second seals the barrel.

game:water-*
amount 5
in target
inventoryAny game:log-placed-*
Pours water into a barrel in batches of five litres, but only when it already contains a log — exactly for tannin.

game:ingot-copper
target ground 3
amount 32

in target
game:ingot-copper 192
output 15
Stacks copper ingots into a column three blocks high and reports 15 on Output once the column is full; one pile holds 64, so three hold 192. As soon as someone starts taking from the pile, Output automatically drops to zero.

from yard to boat

game:ingot-*
amount 16

unload boat

game:firewood
Paper for a Freight Dock with two sections. The first loads ingots directly from the storage yard into the boat, sixteen at a time. The second unloads all firewood from the boat into the Freight Dock crate.

Setting conditions
Write conditions on parchment. Do not sign the parchment so that you can edit its text again.
Transfer conditions into a device by right-clicking it with written parchment. They are saved in the block and shown in its information window when you look at the block. If the device already has conditions, a window first shows the old and new text side by side, and you confirm the overwrite.
Delete conditions from a device with blank parchment: sneak (Shift) and click the block with it. You must confirm deletion as well.
Copy conditions from a device onto blank parchment by clicking the block with it without sneaking.
How to find an item's code and attributes: hold the item in your hand, hold Ctrl, and right-click a device that supports conditions with it. The item's code and attributes usable in conditions are written into the device. Copy them onto blank parchment, edit them into condition blocks, and use them.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosevalve:
The Managed Valve transports liquids through a hose. It always draws the liquid from the distant end of the line to its host. It has one hose anchor and two Signals connectors: the Input controls pumping, and the Output can be controlled using Paper Conditions.

Valve states
• Attached — the valve is placed next to a block with a liquid inventory, such as a barrel, bucket, or campfire. When there is a signal at the Input, it pumps liquid from the distant end of the hose into this host.
• Stand — the valve has no suitable inventory on its mounting side. In this state, it does not transport liquid; as soon as you place a suitable host block next to it, it attaches and starts functioning as an attached valve.
• Spout — a valve placed on the ground. When there is a signal at the Input, it releases liquid from the distant end of the hose; the liquid is not stored in the world, it is only displayed as droplets that soak into the ground. Useful if you need to get rid of excess liquid.

Pump control
Input signals 1 to 7 add a batch of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 liters. Signal 15 pumps continuously. If two Managed Valves are active on one hose, they alternate pumping.
The valve does not transport lava and cools hot water at the destination to the ambient temperature. Paper Conditions can filter the transfer, change the batch size, seal the destination barrel, or set the Output to a value from 0 to 15.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-anchor-occu: This anchor already has a hose.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-same-block: A hose can't connect two anchors of the same block.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hoseintak: The intake is a passive source of water or salt water. Place it in water and connect it with a hose to a Managed valve, which will pump the liquid from it. Longer lines can be extended using hose couplings.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosecoupl: A hose coupling connects two sections of hose and extends the line between Managed valves or intakes. One section of hose can be at most 10 blocks long.
signalslink:item-handbooktext-hose: A hose connects the hose anchors of Managed valves, hose couplings, and intakes. One section can be at most 10 blocks long; couplings allow the line to be extended over a greater distance.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-igniter:
The Igniter lights fires in the adjacent block. When triggered by a signal, it fires a burst of glowing sparks in the direction it is aimed and ignites whatever they land on — a firepit, a pile of logs, or another flammable spot. If the adjacent block is air, the sparks fall downward until they hit a flammable spot or go out after three meters.
It requires charging with temporal gears (Temporal gears) to operate. Insert a gear by clicking it; you can see how many bursts remain in the information window. Every shot costs the same, whether it ignites something or misses.

Connectors
• The input triggers a shot. It responds to the rising edge, meaning a transition from zero to a non-zero value: each signal means exactly one burst of sparks. The igniter deliberately has no continuous mode, so a signal forgotten at fifteen does not burn through the entire supply of gears.
• The output reports the result of the last shot: 1 when ignition succeeded, 0 when it did not or when there was nothing to fire. This can be used to repeat the attempt or send the machine onward.

Aiming
The Igniter can be placed freely, similarly to the Block Sensor, and clicking it switches the aiming direction:
• straight — sparks fly directly in front of the barrel;
• diagonally — sparks fly to the side at an angle, which is useful when something cannot be placed in front of the igniter.
Sparks follow an arc and fly for a while, so the igniter can also reach a spot somewhat lower down. Once the sparks land, the mod checks again what is actually at the landing spot — it may have changed before they get there.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-anchor-oc: This anchor already has a sleeve.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-same-bloc: A sleeve can't connect two anchors of the same block.

signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevedam: The Managed Damper transports items and blocks through a sleeve. It always draws the cargo from the distant end of the line to its host, so the active damper is the one receiving an Input signal. Mounted on a container it fills or empties it; standing on the floor it works with the block it faces, which lets it drop things onto the ground and pick them up again. It has only Input and Output pins - everything else, including slot choice and ground mode, is configured with Paper Conditions.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevecou:
The Sleeve Coupling connects two sections of sleeve, extending the line between Managed Dampers. Each section may be at most 10 blocks long; you may chain together any number of couplings.
The coupling itself controls or transports nothing; it only holds two anchors. Cargo flows through it without restriction and it has no inventory of its own.
To run a line through a wall, encase a completed coupling as a Sleeve Wall Coupling.
signalslink:item-handbooktext-sleeve:
The sleeve is a flexible conduit for items. It connects the sleeve anchors of Managed Dampers and Sleeve Couplings, much like a hose connects valves.
Stretch a sleeve by holding it and clicking two anchors in sequence. One section may be at most 10 blocks long; build longer lines from couplings.
Unlike a hose, a sleeve may not pass through a block. The mod checks its route afterward as well: if someone builds a wall across it or soil collapses into it, the sleeve breaks and the line is interrupted. Keep this in mind for routes near construction sites.
To pass through a wall, use a Sleeve Wall Coupling: connect a separate sleeve section to each opening. The coupling connects the line inside the wall and allows the sealing of a cellar or room to be maintained.
Cut a stretched sleeve with shears.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-too-long: The hose can be at most {0} blocks long.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevewal:
The wall coupling lets you route a sleeve through a wall, floor, or ceiling. It connects just like a regular sleeve coupling.

Switch the seal by Ctrl + right-clicking with a pipe wrench in hand:
• cooling wall — for preserving cellar conditions (default setting);
• insulating wall — for retaining warmth in the room;
• open — without a seal.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-yardsign:
A sign on a post used to name a storage yard. Place it on any tile of the yard and write a name on it.
You do not need ink or a quill to write — the form opens immediately after placement, and you can change the name at any time by clicking it. The name may contain at most 24 characters so that it remains readable from afar.
The yard is named after the first sign standing on it. More signs on one yard are therefore fine, but only one of them determines the name.
The sign is also an ordinary marker — it controls nothing and has no connectors.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-yardtile:
A storage yard tile is ordinary paving on which goods are stacked. It controls nothing by itself and has no state of its own; goods lie on it as ordinary piles on the ground.
A continuous area of these tiles forms a storage yard — a single whole that equipment works with at once instead of having to point at every pile separately.

Shape and size
The shape can be arbitrary as long as the tiles connect by their sides — a rectangle, an L shape, around tracks, or around a building. Tiles that touch only at a corner do not belong to the area.
The area must have at least 4 tiles and at most 400. When the limit is exceeded, the area is considered invalid and this is reported — nothing is cut off halfway.
Two areas that touch anywhere merge into one. If you want two separate ones, leave a gap between them.

How to tell what you built
A raised curb runs along the outer edge of the area, so you can see how far it extends. There is no curb between adjacent tiles, and when you expand the area, it moves to the new edge automatically.
When you look at a tile, the information window states how many tiles the area has. This number is important — it immediately tells you when two areas have accidentally merged into one.

Naming
Place a storage yard sign on the area and write a name on it. The area can then be selected by name, which is useful when you have several next to each other at a station.

How much fits
Each tile holds one column containing one type of goods — for the game, a column is one slot, so its contents do not mix. When a tile holds something else, the equipment skips it and tries the next one.
Only items that can be stacked into a pile belong on the area. Equipment will not place unstackable items there at all — they would lie on the tile as placed blocks and could no longer be picked up.
How tall a column grows is governed by the cargo, not the area: logs can be stacked high, while you want barrels in a single layer so they remain accessible. Vintage Story also has its own restrictions by item type, so some things cannot be stacked that high and the column fills sooner.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-manageddo:
The Freight Dock is a crate that loads and unloads whatever stands next to it: a storage yard, boat, or elk. Unlike other devices, it has two ends. One is the crate itself; the other is the counterpart it finds beside it.
It has one inventory with 48 slots. Every slot accepts items and liquid, so you do not need to worry about what belongs where — Conditions on paper select by contents, not by location.

The paper must say from where to where
A Freight Dock paper is divided into sections. Each section begins with a header that names both ends:
• from X to Y — goods go directly from X to Y. They do not pass through the Freight Dock crate.
• unload X — from X into the Freight Dock crate.
• load X — from the Freight Dock crate into X.
The header must be on its own line and separated from the rules below by a blank line. It applies to all blocks below it, until the next header. Blocks must also be separated from each other by blank lines, as on every paper.
The Freight Dock will not accept paper without a header and will tell you so. An incomplete header is also an error: from boat without to is not treated as unload boat.

Example paper with two sections:
unload boat

game:firewood

load yard north

game:firewood
keep 64
The first section unloads firewood from the boat into the crate. The second places it from the crate onto the yard to the north and keeps 64 pieces there.

Counterparts
After the direction, write which counterpart is meant:
• yard — a storage yard, meaning a continuous paving made of storage yard tiles. A compass direction and a name from a sign may follow the word when you have multiple yards.
• boat — a boat carrying crates, baskets, or chests. The Freight Dock waits until the boat stops. It transfers nothing while it is moving.
• elk — a tamed elk with saddlebags. It can be loaded whenever it is within range.
A compass direction may follow boat and elk, optionally with a distance: north5 means five blocks north of the Freight Dock.
Add-ons may add further counterparts, such as trains.

Header examples:
unload yard — from the nearest yard into the crate
load yard north — from the crate onto the yard to the north
load yard north northern pile — onto the yard to the north named "northern pile"
unload boat west — from the boat to the west into the crate
from yard to elk — from the yard directly into the elk's saddlebags
from boat to yard north — from the boat directly onto the yard to the north

How counterparts are found
Boats and elk are searched for within twelve blocks of the Freight Dock. If several are in range, the nearest is chosen first.
A yard is searched for within ten blocks. Without a direction and with a horizontal direction, it is searched for at the Freight Dock's level and one block below, so the Freight Dock can stand on the yard or beside it.
A compass direction (north, south, east, west) limits the search to that half of the surroundings. Without a direction, the search goes all around.
up and down search for a yard vertically, also within ten blocks: up for a Freight Dock buried below a platform carrying the yard, and down for a Freight Dock above a warehouse whose floor is the yard.
When several yards are in range, the name on the sign decides. Without a name, the nearest one is used.
The entire yard is shown to the paper as one inventory, assembled from columns of stacks from the nearest tile to the farthest. It is therefore filled from your end: the nearest column is filled to its height first, then the next one.

How much is transferred
Without the amount directive, one operation transfers everything that matches the rule. You can therefore unload an entire boat cargo with a single signal.
• amount N — transfers exactly N items, or nothing.
• amount N- — transfers at most N items. If there are fewer goods, whatever is available is transferred. Useful when you want to transfer in batches without stopping when supplies run low.
• amount N+ — transfers at least N items. The Freight Dock waits for a full batch, then moves everything available, up to one stack at a time.
• keep N — keeps N items at the destination. It only adds what is missing up to N.
• height N — how high a column may be stacked on a yard. Logs can be stacked high, while you may want barrels in a single layer so they remain accessible. Some goods cannot be stacked that high, and the column fills sooner.
Note the difference between a condition and keep. The condition in target game:firewood 17- only says whether the block applies. As long as there are fewer than 17 logs at the destination, the block applies and the Freight Dock loads everything it has. If you want to keep seventeen at the destination, write keep 17.

Connectors
• Input provides credit. Signals 1 through 7 add 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 transfers, while signal 15 works continuously. One transfer costs one credit whether it moves one item or a whole stack.
• Output reports what the Freight Dock sees at its ends. Its value is set by blocks with the output directive. They are evaluated across the entire paper, and the first matching one applies, regardless of which section it is written in.
Cancel unspent credit by sneaking and clicking with a wrench.

What an output block asks about
An output block always asks about its section's destination, never its source. In a from yard to boat section, it therefore asks about the boat, not the yard. If you want to report the state of a yard, the yard must be the destination: write the output block in a load yard section. Such a section does not need to transfer anything; the output block alone is enough.
A section whose counterpart is not within range is skipped along with its output blocks. A boat query therefore responds only while a boat is stopped at the Freight Dock. A yard is always in place, so you can query it at any time.

Example:
from yard to boat

game:ingot-*

load yard

game:ingot-* 0
output 15
The first section loads ingots from the yard into the boat. The second transfers nothing and only watches the yard: as soon as no ingots remain on it, Output shows 15.

Placement
The Freight Dock is placed rotated like a crate or chest: it is placed with its connectors facing you, in one of sixteen rotations. It transfers nothing without a signal on Input.

signalslink:block-handbooktext-chunkanch:
The anchor keeps a piece of the world loaded even when nobody is there. Without it, a remote factory stops the moment you leave it and starts up again when you return.
Click to open a map of the surrounding area. The anchor is in the middle; it keeps the lighter squares loaded; click them to turn them on and off. The column the anchor stands in is always kept loaded. Zoom the map with the mouse wheel and pan it by dragging.
In the same window, you can name the anchor so you can recognize it in the server log, and turn it off with the Anchor enabled switch without having to dig it up. The server administrator decides how many columns one anchor may keep loaded; usually it is 64.

What it costs
The anchor consumes temporal gears. The cost increases according to how much it keeps running: the number of active blocks and domestic animals in the kept chunks.
An active block is a block that works on its own: a furnace, barrel, beehive, field, mill, machines, and devices. Chests, crates, and other storage blocks also count, because the game tracks goods spoilage in them. Doors, chiselled blocks, and piles of goods on the ground do not count, no matter how many there are.
An animal counts only if it is domestic, meaning born in captivity, or if it is a tamed moose. Wild animals and monsters do not count. One animal costs as much as two active blocks.
Each kept column also costs something by itself, even if there is nothing in it — a loaded chunk uses memory and is saved. So keeping empty chunks loaded just in case is not worthwhile.
The cost rises more steeply than proportionally, so a small remote workshop is cheap while a home base is absurdly expensive. The anchor is useful for a remote workshop, not for an entire castle.
You can see the cost on the map and in the block description before inserting a gear. When you are standing by the anchor, it consumes nothing — those chunks would be loaded anyway.
Give the anchor a gear by clicking it while holding one. One extra fits in the slot as a reserve; it can also be supplied by a Managed Chute. When both the charge and reserve run out, the anchor releases everything and waits for someone to bring it a gear.

Fields and animals
Fields in kept chunks grow and ripen even when nobody is near them. The same applies to bushes and fruit trees. Every tilled soil block is an active block, so a large field affects the cost.
Wild plants and grass in kept chunks do not grow; that happens only around players.
Domestic animals are social creatures and merely stand around without a person nearby. As long as no player is within roughly 128 blocks, they do not eat from the trough or breed. Young animals still grow up, and pregnant females give birth. Animals do not die of hunger.
Breeding by an anchor therefore does not multiply on its own: you must care for the herd personally. The anchor is useful for machines and fields, not for an automatic animal farm.

Sleeping
The anchor does not have to keep loaded all the time. In the anchor window, set how often it wakes up and how long it stays awake — between those times, it sleeps and costs nothing.
• Waking up: never sleeps, every hour, every 4 hours, every 24 hours, or only on trigger. These are game hours.
• How long awake: 15, 30, 60, or 120 minutes of game time.
This is useful for a factory that operates only occasionally: the anchor wakes up, the chunks load, a train arrives and unloads raw materials, and production starts. A production sensor then holds a signal on the anchor's input, and as long as the signal lasts, the anchor does not sleep. Once the raw materials run out and the signal goes off, the anchor sleeps again when the awake period expires.
The awake period should therefore not be short — it must allow not only for the train's arrival, but also for the factory sensors to wake up and manage to report something.
A switch can make the anchor wake up whenever someone joins an empty server. While nobody is on the server, time does not pass and no interval elapses.
The Wake only on trigger option means that the anchor sleeps after its awake period and the clock will no longer wake it — only a signal on the input, a player's arrival (if enabled), or an arriving vehicle (if enabled) can wake it. A wire on the input wakes a sleeping anchor only if its other end is in a loaded chunk.

Trains
If a train mod is installed, the Wake when a train approaches switch is added: a sleeping anchor wakes up as soon as a train is heading for its station, and does not sleep until it arrives. This loads the chunks before the train arrives, allowing the train to appear at the station and unload.
Example: a train carrying raw materials travels to a remote factory. Set Wake only on trigger, 120 minutes awake, and enable Wake when a train approaches. The anchor sleeps and costs nothing until the train sets off for its station. Then it wakes up, the train unloads, and as long as the production sensor holds a signal on the input, the anchor does not sleep.
The selected columns must cover the entire stationary train, not just the station. A train appears at the station only when the chunks beneath all its cars are loaded. A train that does not fit within the kept columns simply passes through the station and unloads nothing. A three-car train usually needs two columns, and if the station is at a chunk boundary, even three. When this happens, the anchor writes it to the server log.
The anchor never splits a stationary train: it also keeps loaded any columns its cars extend into until it leaves — they are charged like any other kept column — and it does not sleep while a train is standing in its area.
The SignalsLink.YTT mod keeps trains together. If Yang's Transport Tycoon is on the server without it, anchors disable themselves: an anchor could leave a train half loaded and it would get stuck. Instead of controls, the anchor then shows what needs to be installed; its settings remain saved and are restored automatically after installation.

Disabled by administrator
The server administrator can disable anchors completely with the AnchorsEnabled option in the signalslink.json file. The anchor then keeps nothing loaded, costs nothing, and says that an administrator disabled it. All anchor settings remain saved, so they continue where they left off when enabled again.

Connectors
Input — a signal on it prevents sleeping.
Output — reports the gear state from 0 to 15. Useful for an indicator light or a chute that supplies the anchor with a gear when it is running low.
